title: Teaching by walking through cheese
summary: He explains his method of teaching a laid-back blues feel and his Lincoln Center workshops.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: and this idea flashes in my head to have him just walking through cheese. Because I was thinking about this thing. There’s a resistance. You know when you play music, like to learn jazz violin you really have to learn about what it’s like to play a horn. Because things come too easy. You know people that can play really well, you know it’s harder to learn to swing. And I think about like Ellington’s band, they could really lay back, but the rhythm section stayed right there — the difference between that and a band that’s just dragging. So there’s this like tension between it. So I would have them walk through cheeses like you’d have to walk. I mean like visualize, my apartment is like Swiss cheese. And every movement is like this. And I’m talking about like an hour and a half or an hour fifteen minutes like this, and I would teach them a song after they got acclimated to this idea. And I said, “When you sing back to me,” and mind you I’d never done this before.
You’re making it up as you go along, yeah.

Yeah, and I’ll be honest. I mean it’s not that I don’t take credit but through meditation and stuff like this, things just come through and you can’t — I think you lose it when you say oh isn’t it great what I came up with. But it came through, and I take credit for being the vessel for it. So basically he comes through in the house and I sing a song called “Wanderlust,” do you know this? An old blues by Duke. [scats]. You know it’s really laid back blues. And I would teach it phrase by phrase, and have them sing it. But then you can’t get the sound. [scats]. I ended up doing this with groups of like 40 people. And other ideas have come. So they’ll do that to the point where they can sing that like an old blues band, and I say okay, now get the horn. But you know what always happens? They forget they’re in cheese. They walk around, gee, you can’t walk that fast in cheese. That’s why I always let those lessons go longer because it takes — and they do the same thing, sing that thing then play it on the horn, and then we move, after all that, you know, we move to the piano and sing it, and I’ll play the chords, and then improvise. Usually when they start improvising they go back to just how they sounded before, maybe a little better.

I mean the first two sound like some old black man doing his blues. And you can see in their faces they’re blown away. So I mean early on, it’s been twenty years probably, since that started. I saw there is a way to really find ways to get the sound out. Like I sing in the car [scats] you can learn that. And there’s nothing wrong with making new language. But finding your inner voice. So it’s really been a blessing and a gift to me. Like I go into a room and I’ve been doing a lot of stuff at Lincoln Center, not the Jazz at Lincoln Center but they have visitor services like where a big band will come from Chicago and they’ll tour Lincoln Center and then have a workshop with me and their concert band will have a workshop with someone else.
